newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Senior Japan banker optimistic about Tokyo market.
newsitem.headline: Senior Japan banker optimistic about Tokyo market.

text.p: Toyoo Gyohten, senior advisor to the world's largest bank, Japan's Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi Ltd, said he was reasonably optimistic about the Tokyo stock market and the market's recovery today was natural.

Gyohten, a former vice minister at Japan's influential Ministry of Finance, also said he expected the Bank of Japan (BOJ) to continue its current easy monetary policy stance until there are clear signs of recovery.
Gyohten, former chairman of the Bank of Tokyo, spoke to reporters near the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), central bank to the worlds' central banks.
Toru Hashimoto, president of Fuji Bank Ltd, was also in Basle and told reporters that the recovery in Japan's stock market was "good news." He said he did not know if the market would go higher.

Tokyo's Nikkei 225 index has dropped sharply since the beginning of the year and plunged another 4.26 percent last Friday on worries about the economic outlook, the pace of structural reform in Japan and the health of financial firms.
On Monday, however, the Tokyo stock market recovered in what Tokyo brokers described as a mostly technical advance.
The Nikkei average rose 815.14 points, or 4.71 percent, on Monday to finish at 18,118.79.
Central bank governors from the Group of 10 (G10) leading industrial nations meet 10 times a year at the Basle-based BIS to discuss international and monetary affairs.
BIS also houses the Basle Committee on Banking Supervision, which oversees the health of international banks.

Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer, who is also chairman of the G10 central bank governors' committee, told reporters that there had been an informal discussion on Sunday between banking supervisors and leading bankers from Japan, the U.S., England, Germany and France.

At their meeting, G10 had discussed the situation in Japan's financial markets, but Tietmeyer declined to specify the content of the discussions. Today's G10 meeting included Bank of Japan governor Yasuo Matsushita and U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan. Matsushita and Greenspan normally only attend the G10 meetings at the BIS three or four times a year.
Matsushita and Greenspan declined to respond to reporters' questions.
Gyohten said there had been a variety of reasons for the recent decline in the Tokyo stock market, but there was no clear reasons for the sharp fall.
"I think it was natural for the market to come back strongly this morning," Gyohten said.
He expected the recovery of Japan's economy to continue to be slow, partially due to the challenge of improving the government's fiscal situation.

"Because of the efforts on the fiscal side, I am afraid the overall growth for 1997 could be slightly below 1996," Gyohten said, adding that he wanted to stress that the fundamental recovery process was still going on.

On Friday Japanese authorities warned the market not to expect any government bailout and Gyohten said this move demonstrated the government's new policy of letting markets find their own levels without any interference.
"The recent events indicated that markets are prepared to accept that as a matter of life," Gyohten said.
Gyohten said it was very difficult to predict how markets would continue to behave, noting the sharp swings from highs in 1990 to lows in 1995.
However, comparing corporate profitability now with the situation in 1995, Gyohten said it is clear profits are better now.
"That is enough reason to allow us to be reasonably optimistic," he said.
Given the fiscal problems faced by Japan, Gyohten said his personal feeling was that there was very little room for monetary policy to be more restrictive.
"My guess is that the current easing of monetary policy needs to be maintained for some time, until there are clear signs of a strong recovery in the market situation," he said.
